attribution.note: Marcus wrote this himself in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'most', the three content categories taken from the context, and the comparative jailbreak qualifier. It is a present-tense comparative observation.

contract.note: The plain reading (comparative susceptibility under ordinary or light prompting, a majority of major model families) is ordinary and fair. The model set and the effort threshold come from the evaluator, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: A contemporary CNN test found Gemini and ChatGPT refused a light prompt that drew antisemitism from Grok 4. It covers only two alternatives and one category, so it cannot settle the majority claim.
The ADL's March 2025 bias study covers an earlier period and uses broad bias measures, not the specified outputs or jailbreak effort.

reviews.rationale: The only contemporary comparison fits Marcus's claim in a narrow way: two alternatives refused where Grok complied. But it covers neither a majority of major models nor the Hitler and sexual-violence categories. The ADL findings come from an earlier period and use a different measure. The packet does not settle the comparison.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully restates an evaluative observation about the Grok 4 launch period.

contract.note: Reading 'can't stop' as a practical failure that continued through the launch period is fair. Requiring persistence after mitigation is the evaluator's reading of 'can't stop', and it drives the result.

evidence.note: CNN got antisemitic Grok 4 output repeatedly over several days, which shows dark invective did occur. But the same prompt had stopped working by Sunday, which cuts against 'can't stop'. Test dates are unspecified.
xAI's July 15 statement about itself admits Grok 4 problems (the MechaHitler surname issue) and reports prompt fixes. A self-reported fix proves neither persistence nor success.
This concerns the July 8 incident on the @grok bot, before the period being judged and on a different surface.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows Grok 4 produced dark antisemitic output during the launch window, and xAI admitted problems. The contract, though, needs abusive output to persist after mitigation, and the packet does not show that. CNN's test prompt had stopped eliciting it by July 13, and xAI's fix was self-reported. The 'can't stop' part is therefore not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'hardly' and 'effective'. The world-domination clause is close to rhetorical but is stated firmly.

contract.note: The plain reading of AGI and the strategic-planning reading are ordinary. Because both clauses are required, the evaluator's interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Grok 4 scored 15.9% on ARC-AGI-2 in July 2025, a large gap on one benchmark of unfamiliar reasoning, though it was a new top score. It does not speak to world-domination planning.
The benchmark paper's human baseline (about 66% average) helps interpret the gap. It is background only.
Strong long-horizon results on Vending-Bench caution against assuming Grok cannot plan, but the page was updated later and does not test anything like world domination.
xAI's launch announcement about its own model claims strong capabilities. That is not independent and does not show AGI.

reviews.rationale: The ARC-AGI-2 result partly supports 'a long way from AGI' on one benchmark. No evidence addresses whether Grok could devise a workable world-domination strategy, and the contract needs both clauses supported. The capability evidence goes both ways. The case remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation of Musk's launch remarks. Musk's quoted words are only the object of the claim.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps only 'doesn't know how to control' and drops the other two things Marcus says Musk admitted: that AI might be bad, and that he would like to be around to watch. That narrows what Marcus committed to.

contract.note: Allowing a substantive paraphrase while treating uncertainty about outcomes as different from admitting lack of control is fair. 'Basically admitted' is still interpretive, so the reading drives the result.

evidence.note: In this third-party transcript Musk voices uncertainty and acceptance ('like to be alive to see it'), which supports the omitted clauses. It contains no admission that he does not know how to control his AI.

reviews.rationale: The transcript supports Marcus's statements that Musk said AI might be bad and that he would like to be alive to see it. It does not show Musk admitting he does not know how to control his AI; that is Marcus's own inference. The control part is contradicted and the other parts hold, so the outcome is mixed.
